Article Title: Govt proposes mandatory Vehicle-to-Vehicle communication systems from Oct 2028 to cut road crashes
Article Text:
All new cars, passenger and goods vehicles would need to have Vehicle-to-Vehicle communication system. (PTI)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: From Oct 2028, all new two- and three-wheelers, cars, passenger and goods vehicles (including buses and trucks) would need to have Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communication system, as per a draft notification of the road transport ministry. The V2V technology is being rolled out to curb collisions and accidents.The recently published draft notification by road transport ministry proposes phased implementation of the V2V communication system and to start with all vehicles in categories L (two- and three-wheelers), M (passenger vehicles) and N (goods vehicles) manufactured from Oct 2027 would be required to comply with the newly-notified automotive standard, AIS-230, wherever they are equipped with V2V communication systems.The technology enables real-time exchange of speed, direction, position, and braking data between vehicles to prevent collisions at blind curves, intersections, or from drivers coming the wrong way without needing a cellular network. Each vehicle needs to be fitted with a device that will automatically detect approaching vehicles for preventing any crash.Unlike conventional vehicle-safety systems, which primarily depend on onboard sensors and driver reaction, V2V communication can provide information beyond the direct line of sight.“It is therefore expected to complement Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) and support proactive accident prevention, connected mobility and future intelligent transport applications,” the ministry said.In this case, every vehicle fitted with the V2V communication system will continuously send out their locations, speed and direction as tiny radio signals. They will also relay information on sudden braking by a vehicle ahead, forward collision risks, unsafe lane changes, wrong-way driving and the approach of emergency vehicles.The receiving vehicle’s system compares this information with its own location, speed and direction to predict a possible collision and alerts the driver for action.At a later stage, govt will also roll out the Vehicle to Infrastructure (V2I) communication system. In this case, sensors are installed with infrastructure, such as signal and power poles, edges of bridges and flyovers, and barricaded areas to alert vehicles.
Article Summary: All new cars, passenger and goods vehicles would need to have Vehicle-to-Vehicle communication system. The V2V technology is being rolled out to curb collisions and accidents. Each vehicle needs to be fitted with a device that will automatically detect approaching vehicles for preventing any crash.

Article Title: Census phase 2 likely to accept half-filled forms
Article Text:
In the first phase of the census — involving housing and houselisting operations — those opting for self-enumeration were not able to submit the form with blank fields

NEW DELHI: Census authorities are considering allowing persons self-enumerating for the population enumeration phase of Census 2027 to submit a partially filled form online.In the first phase of the census - involving housing and houselisting operations - those opting for self-enumeration were not able to submit the form with blank fields. If any field was left blank - either accidentally or intentionally due to lack of clarity - the user could not advance to the submission window.Sources said that it was felt during discussions among census teams that this feature forced many to opt out of self-enumeration and rely on the enumerator's visit to record their replies to the questionnaire.There is now a realisation that even a partially filled form, provided a minimum number of questions are answered, would help in easing the task of the enumerator. Besides, self-declared data tends to be more accurate and reliable."Internal deliberations focused on why the self-enumeration option should not be made flexible, given that the data is to be entered digitally either by the respondent or the enumerator.The census application anyway allows the enumerator to access the filled-up form and change any wrongly entered data. So why can't he access a partially filled-up form and fill in the few remaining fields during the house visit, saving time and effort?" an officer told TOI.The population enumeration exercise is set to be conducted nationwide in Feb 2027. However, the exercise, as per convention, is advanced for select states/UTs like Ladakh, J&K, HP and Uttarakhand that become wholly or partially snow-bound in Feb. These areas will witness population enumeration from Sept 1 to 30, preceded by a self-enumeration window of Aug 17-30.
Article Summary: In the first phase of the census, those opting for self-enumeration were not able to submit the form with blank fields. If any field was left blank - either accidentally or intentionally - the user could not advance to the submission window. There is now a realisation that even a partially filled form, provided a minimum number of questions are answered, would help ease the task of the enumerator.

Article Title: How to download Minecraft Bedrock 26.40 update on all platforms
Article Text:
Minecraft Bedrock 26.40 update has been released (Image via Mojang)

How to download Minecraft Bedrock 26.40 update

Windows 10/11 (PC)

Open the Minecraft Launcher on your PC and select the Minecraft: Bedrock Edition from the sidebar.

Next, ensure that the drop-down menu next to the Play button is set to the Latest Release.

The launcher will automatically fetch and download build 26.40.

Xbox One and Xbox Series X|S

Navigate to My Games & Apps from your main Xbox dashboard.

Highlight Minecraft, press the Menu button (three horizontal lines) on your controller, and select Manage game and add-ons.

Select Updates and initiate the download for the 26.40 patch. If you have automatic updates enabled in your system settings, the game may have already updated.

PlayStation 4 and PlayStation 5

Locate Minecraft on your PlayStation home screen or within your Game Library.

Press the Options button on your DualShock or DualSense controller.

Select Check for Update from the side menu. The console will automatically find, download, and install version 26.40.

Nintendo Switch

Hover over Minecraft on the home menu and click on either the “+” or “-” button on your controller.

After the Options menu opens up, tap on “Software Update” and select the Via the Internet option.

Your Switch will search and download the Minecraft Bedrock 26.40 update.

Pocket Edition (Android and iOS)

Android (Google Play Store)

Open the Google Play Store app and tap on your profile icon in the top right corner.

Select Manage apps & device, then navigate to the Updates available section.

Find Minecraft in the pending list and tap Update.

iOS (Apple App Store)

Open the App Store and tap your profile icon in the top right corner.

Scroll down to refresh the page and view your pending app updates.

Locate Minecraft and tap the Update button next to it to begin the download.

What’s news in the Minecraft Bedrock 26.40 update?

Dappled Forests and Abandoned Camps

Players can now toggle on the Drop 3 experimental features to explore the brand-new Dappled Forest biome. This biome features Poplar Trees (which drop orange, red, and yellow leaves), decorative Red Shrubs, and bouncy Shelf Mushrooms.

While exploring, you will also stumble upon Abandoned Camp structures. These camps now generate across 18 different biomes, featuring unique, biome-specific designs and procedural trees alongside hidden loot chests.

New Items and Blocks

Base building and interior design just got a major upgrade. The update introduces Wool Stairs and Wool Slabs in all 16 standard colors. You can also craft the Cushion, which is an interactive item you can actually sit on. For explorers, the new single-use Straw Bed (crafted from Hay Bales) allows you to safely sleep through the night without permanently resetting your established spawn point.

Gameplay and Parity Changes

Significant parity adjustments have been implemented to match Java Edition mechanics. Boats now naturally regenerate damage and require fewer hits to break. Combat has also been refined: arrow damage now scales intelligently with velocity instead of being fully randomized, and Arrows of Harming no longer bounce off entities. Furthermore, Minecart entity separation has been restored, and dozens of graphical, UI, and performance bugs have been successfully squashed.

The highly anticipated Minecraft Bedrock 26.40 update is here, and it has introduced massive wave of bug fixes, gameplay adjustments, and the Drop 3 experimental features. From discovering the colorful new Dappled Forest to experiencing key combat parity changes with Java Edition, this release is filled with new content for survival players, builders, and technical creators alike.To enjoy all the new features added to Minecraft as part of the 26.40 update, you can download it on your devices. The next section gives you a detailed guide on the same:The Minecraft Bedrock 26.40 update is rolling out worldwide across all supported platforms. Here is exactly how you can download it on your device of choice:This was all you needed to know about downloading the Minecraft Bedrock 26.40 update.
Article Summary: The highly anticipated Minecraft Bedrock 26.40 update is here. It has introduced massive wave of bug fixes, gameplay adjustments, and the Drop 3 experimental features. The update is rolling out worldwide across all supported platforms. Here is exactly how you can download it on your device.

Article Title: Hack of the Day: Cut your TV bill by optimising channels using the TRAI app
Article Text:
TRAI

What it solves



What to do



Steps to follow



A quick note before you start



Most DTH and cable subscribers have, at some point, glanced at their monthly bill and wondered why it keeps creeping up even though their viewing habits haven't changed. The usual culprit isn't a price hike from the operator — it's unused channels and bouquets that were added at some point, forgotten about, and never removed. TRAI's Channel Selector app was built specifically to fix this, and yet most people who could benefit from it have never opened it.Under TRAI's tariff framework, subscribers pay for bouquets and individual channels, and operators have little incentive to proactively trim a customer's list down to only what they watch. Over months or years, subscriptions tend to accumulate: a bouquet added for one sports season that was never removed, regional channels bundled in by default, or add-ons picked during a promotional offer that quietly continue at full price afterward. The result is a bill that has drifted upward without any real increase in what's actually being watched. The fix isn't negotiating with the operator — it's simply seeing the full list and removing what isn't needed.The TRAI Channel Selector app puts that full list in front of you and lets you edit it directly. It works across most major DTH and cable operators, including Tata Play, Airtel Digital TV, DishTV, d2h, and Hathway, and connects straight to your operator's system to pull your current plan and push through changes once you've made them.1. Install the app or visit the portal. The TRAI Channel Selector app is available on the Google Play Store and Apple App Store, or accessible through the web portal if you'd rather not download anything.2. Select your DTH provider and log in. Choose your operator from the list, then log in using your registered TV number, subscriber ID, or set-top box number, followed by an OTP sent to your registered mobile or displayed on screen.3. View your current subscription. Once logged in, the app shows a full breakdown: active bouquets, individual channels, total channel count, and your current monthly cost. This step alone is often the most useful part — many users are surprised by how many channels are sitting in their plan unwatched.4. Select only the channels you watch. Go through the list and uncheck anything that doesn't get used. The app also suggests optimised bouquet combinations that can lower your total cost while keeping the channels you actually want.5. Submit the optimised pack to your operator. Confirm the changes and submit. You'll receive an acknowledgment number along with your revised monthly bill, and the update is typically reflected on your connection within about 72 hours.Operator support and login methods can vary slightly — some ask for a subscriber ID instead of a registered mobile number, and the exact wording of menus differs by provider. If a screen doesn't match exactly what's described above, it's worth following the in-app prompts for your specific operator rather than assuming something's gone wrong.
Article Summary: TRAI's Channel Selector app lets you see and edit your DTH and cable bill. It works across most major operators, including Tata Play, Airtel Digital TV, DishTV, d2h, and Hathway. The app suggests optimised bouquet combinations that can lower your total cost while keeping the channels you actually want.

Article Title: From apps to 'intent': How AI agents will rewrite the way we use next‑generation smartphones
Article Text:
The era of app icon grids on smartphones is ending soon. AI-first phones will use agents to fulfill user intents directly.

The era of scrolling through grids of colourful icons and hunting for the 'right' app is ending.

What is an AI-first phone?

AI-first smartphones promise a radically different future — one where users rarely think about apps at all.

What will it look like?

A day with an AI‑first phone

App-centric workflow: You decide to take a last-minute weekend trip. You open a search engine to find destinations, launch a travel aggregator app to search flights, hop into a hotel app to compare rooms, open a weather app to pack appropriately, and manually copy-paste reservation details into your calendar and communication apps. You tap dozens of buttons and navigate through multiple distinct user interfaces.

You decide to take a last-minute weekend trip. You open a search engine to find destinations, launch a travel aggregator app to search flights, hop into a hotel app to compare rooms, open a weather app to pack appropriately, and manually copy-paste reservation details into your calendar and communication apps. You tap dozens of buttons and navigate through multiple distinct user interfaces. The AI-first workflow: You simply say, "Find me a relaxing beach getaway for this weekend under Rs20,000 total, handle the bookings, and make sure I’m home by Sunday night for dinner."

"Flight booked on Carrier X, room reserved at Hotel Y, total cost Rs18,780. Confirm payment via Biometrics?"

This might all sound like sci-fi, but phones with such capabilities are already on the way.

What this means for platforms, business models

No downloads, no updates: Users won't install a parking app, they will ask an AI agent to pay for parking, and it will fetch the operator's terms and then complete the payment.

Users won't install a parking app, they will ask an AI agent to pay for parking, and it will fetch the operator's terms and then complete the payment. One interface, many back‑ends: The conversational layer replaces hundreds of bespoke interfaces. The value shifts from designing a tap‑heavy UI to ensuring your service is reliably callable by AI agents, which means having a robust Application Programming Interface (API), a set of rules that lets different softwares talk to each other.

The conversational layer replaces hundreds of bespoke interfaces. The value shifts from designing a tap‑heavy UI to ensuring your service is reliably callable by AI agents, which means having a robust Application Programming Interface (API), a set of rules that lets different softwares talk to each other. Discovery moves from stores to agents: Instead of optimising for store rankings, companies will optimise for being the agent's trusted choice — based on price, reliability, speed, and policy compliance.

App stores as service registries: Stores may evolve into curated directories of agent‑callable services (APIs) with verified security, privacy, and compliance badges — less about installs, more about trust.

Stores may evolve into curated directories of agent‑callable services (APIs) with verified security, privacy, and compliance badges — less about installs, more about trust. Monetisation shifts: Revenue models may tilt toward per‑action fees, subscriptions, and revenue share on agent‑completed transactions rather than one‑time downloads or ad‑heavy freemium apps.

Developer pivot: Teams will build "agent skills" and robust APIs, not just UIs. The competitive edge becomes reliability, speed, and transparent pricing that AI agents can compare.

The end of the app as we know it?

For nearly two decades, our relationship with mobile technology has been governed by a single, undisputed design: the app icon grid.Ever since Apple launched the App Store in 2008, the burden of digital logistics has rested firmly on the user.Need a taxi? Open an app. Want to order dinner? Open another app. Pay a bill? Another app. Book a flight, check the news, edit a photo, send money, check your fitness, reserve a hotel, translate a menu, buy groceries — there is an app for everything.The modern smartphone is essentially a container filled with hundreds of miniature software silos, each demanding its own login, interface, permissions, subscriptions and updates.App Store and Google Play became the gateways to this digital universe, spawning a multi-billion-dollar economy that transformed companies like Apple and Google into the world's most powerful software gatekeepers.This model is about to collapse.The era of scrolling through grids of colourful icons and hunting for the 'right' app is ending.We are on the precipice of the biggest shift in consumer technology since the multi-touch screen: the rise of the 'AI-first' smartphone.Today's smartphones are built around apps because software was designed for humans to navigate manually. Every service has its own interface. Every company competes for a permanent place on the home screen. Success is measured by daily active users opening an app multiple times a day.AI-first smartphones promise a radically different future — one where users rarely think about apps at all.The devices are designed around small language models (SLMs) and multimodal AI agents that will run locally on your phone for quick, privacy‑sensitive tasks; and hand-off heavier reasoning to edge or cloud computing.The phones will discard the traditional operating system architecture of home screens, file systems, and sandboxed apps.In their place will be an 'Intent Engine' — a continuous, real-time operating layer powered by AI agents.Instead of interacting with software through apps, users will express their intent to AI agents.When a user expresses a goal — whether spoken, typed, or inferred through context — the phone's core AI agent will break down that intent into logical sub-tasks, assign actions to underlying services, and compile the result into a custom, dynamically generated view.In practice, the home screen will become a goal launcher, not an app grid.You might see tiles like 'Plan my weekend', 'What's in the news?', or 'Track expenses', each invoking an agent that orchestrates the underlying services.Without the structural necessity of cramming dozens of app icons onto a home screen, phone hardware can evolve beyond the glass slab.While touchscreens will remain vital for rich visual consumption, hardware design will prioritise contextual inputs: micro-cameras, directional arrays, health sensors, and ambient displays. The primary interface becomes voice, gesture, and subtle visual cues.Because the device is powered by an overarching agent rather than hundreds of disparate software platforms, phone performance will be pristine. Storage constraints shift from managing gigabytes of cached app binaries to hosting optimised, localised neural networks.Consider a typical scenario on a contemporary device versus an AI-first phone:The phone’s AI agent does not "open" an app. It queries hundreds of services simultaneously.It evaluates airline availability, checks boutique hotel inventory, verifies your personal calendar for conflicts, pulls your saved dietary preferences for in-flight meals, and presents a single, unified execution card:With one tap or voice confirmation, the entire transaction settles.You never browsed an app, never logged into a third-party interface, and never manually transferred a single byte of data.When you arrive at the airport the agent surfaces your boarding pass and gate changes without you opening an airline or travel app or email.When you land, the AI agent has already arranged a rental car for your transport.When you need to pay a parking fee, it identifies the lot operator, fetches terms, and pays via biometric authentication — no apps required.Over time, the phone learns your preferences and constraints, making these interactions faster and more anticipatory.Health apps would stop being destinations and become background services.Instead of jumping between sleep, fitness, medication, diet, and doctor apps, you could simply say, “Help me recover from a bad week of sleep” or “Book the earliest endocrinologist in my network,” and the phone would pull data from wearables, records, pharmacies, labs, and calendars to act on your behalf.That would make health management far more proactive. The phone could spot problems early — a rising resting heart rate, missed medication, or a sleep pattern going off track — and respond before you even open an app.The same shift would hit financial apps even harder.Rather than using separate banking, payments, budgeting, tax, and bill-pay apps, you could say, “Pay my credit card, move the rest to savings, and warn me if travel spending goes over budget,” and the phone would handle it in the background.This might all sound like sci-fi, but phones with such capabilities are already in the advanced production stage and the underlying technology has already been proven. As AI automates more of our routine digital interactions, the focus will shift from managing apps to engaging with curated experiences, from structured wellness journeys to step-by-step lessons in finance and investing The app store model has been the single most lucrative cash cow in modern technology history.Platforms like Apple and Google extract up to a 30% commission on digital purchases, while controlling distribution, user acquisition, and developer access.The rise of agentic AI threatens to disassemble this walled-garden economy entirely.Market research firm Gartner last year projected that mobile app usage will drop 25% by 2027 as AI assistants absorb routine tasks, a trend already visible in how people use AI tools instead of opening multiple apps for research, drafting, and scheduling.App stores were built for a world where software arrived as siloed products with their own user interfaces (UI) and update cycles.AI agents invert that model:The app economy won't vanish overnight, but its centre of gravity will move:Brands will no longer compete on who has the slickest app design or the most addicting engagement loops; they will compete on execution speed, data reliability, and service quality.A food delivery service won't win customers by optimising 'dark patterns' in its app; it will win because its backend API offers the fastest delivery times and lowest rates when an AI agent compares options on behalf of a user.Businesses won't simply ask:"How do we rank first on Google?"They'll ask:"How do we become our customer's AI's preferred choice?"Predictions about the death of apps should be treated cautiously. Email survived instant messaging. Websites survived social media. Desktop software survived cloud computing.Apps are unlikely to vanish completely.Many professional tools, creative applications, games and specialised software will still benefit from rich, dedicated user interfaces. A graphic designer editing a complex image or a gamer playing a visually intensive title will continue to rely on purpose-built applications.But for the vast majority of everyday smartphone interactions, the trend points in a different direction.Booking travel, paying bills, getting news updates, shopping, scheduling appointments, managing subscriptions and countless other routine tasks are increasingly suited to conversational AI that can coordinate multiple services behind the scenes.Just as few people think about the networking protocols that power the internet, future users may stop thinking about apps altogether. They will simply tell their phones what they want, and the AI will decide how to make it happen.If the smartphone era was defined by tapping icons, the next chapter may be defined by something far simpler: asking.And when software becomes something you ask rather than something you open, the app store no longer sits at the center of the mobile experience. It becomes the plumbing behind it.For users, the payoff is simplicity: fewer icons, fewer logins, fewer steps.For builders, the mandate is clear: design for agents — reliable APIs, transparent pricing, and policies that make your service the obvious trustable choice when the phone decides on the user's behalf.
Article Summary: The era of app icon grids on smartphones is ending soon. AI-first phones will use agents to fulfill user intents directly. The value shifts from designing a tap‑heavy UI to ensuring your service is reliably callable by AI agents.

Article Title: Scientists have built robot that has one practical mission: Keeping tabs on great white shark to protect swimmers
Article Text:
Representative Image of a futuristic robot

Shark-spotting robots said to monitor a beach for up to a week

Drone to provide an aerial view of the water

Scientists in California are reportedly developing a semi-autonomous robot designed to detect great white sharks near beaches and give researchers and lifeguards more information about their movements. According to a report by the New York Post, researchers at California State University, Long Beach’s Shark Lab have unveiled the Shark Surveillance Bot (SSB), which can patrol waters just offshore. Once fully operational, the robot will “listen” for great white sharks fitted with tracking tags. At the same time, it will collect water samples to search for shark environmental DNA, or eDNA — genetic traces that sharks leave in the water through skin cells, blood and other biological material.The project is being developed by the Shark Lab in collaboration with New York University’s Center of Robotics and the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute. It is funded by the Seaver Institute. The robots, the lab said will “be capable of patrolling off a beach, listening for tagged white sharks, sampling water for shark eDNA, and will have a drone nest on the back for aerial surveillance”.As stated in the report, researchers hope the Shark Surveillance Bot will eventually be able to remain near an individual beach for as long as a week, continuously gathering information about sharks in the area.The aim is not simply to detect whether a shark is nearby. Scientists want to better understand which sharks are present and how many are moving around popular beaches.“Our data suggests that there are sharks around our beaches all the time without incident,” Shark Lab Director Christopher Lowe told KTLA as quoted in the report. “Knowing what sharks, and how many are out there helps lifeguards make better decisions in beach safety operations and in advising the public.”The robot will detect signals from great white sharks that researchers have previously fitted with tracking tags. Its water-sampling system will provide another way of looking for evidence of sharks through environmental DNA.The shark-monitoring robot will also work with an aerial drone. The drone will sit on the robot and can be launched to provide researchers with a bird’s-eye view of the surrounding ocean. The system will combine this aerial footage with 360-degree video and shark-tracking data. Information can then be sent back to the Shark Lab over Wi-Fi.Researchers hope the technology could eventually provide lifeguards with near real-time information about shark activity, helping them make beach safety decisions based on more detailed data.
Article Summary: Shark-spotting robots said to monitor a beach for up to a week. Drone to provide an aerial view of the water for more detailed data. Technology could eventually provide lifeguards with near real-time information about shark activity, helping them make beach safety decisions.

Article Title: WhatsApp accounts put under review for 24 hour: When WhatsApp account is put under review, how to appeal
Article Text:
Multiple WhatsApp accounts put under review for over 24 hour

Information about temporarily banned accounts on WhatsApp

How to send a WhatsApp account review request

Open app and tap on Send review request .

Once WhatsApp reviews your account and makes a decision, you'll receive a notification on WhatsApp.

Why a WhatsApp account is banned

Meta-owned WhatsApp has put multiple accounts, including those in India, under review for 24 hours. According to a report by PTI, access to all app features for the impacted accounts have been blocked, prompting users to flag the issue on social media platforms. Users reported seeing the following message on WhatsApp app screen: "Account in review. Date requested: 3 Aug 2026. Your account activity and device info is being checked to make sure it follows our terms of service. We will notify you of the result typically within 24 hours." The disruption was highlighted around 8 pm IST when users took to Elon Musk-owned X flagging the issue. "My WhatsApp account has been disabled without any explanation. I have already submitted an appeal, but the review page only displays a generic message stating that it will "typically be reviewed within 24 hours. Help me urgently," one user tweeted.Responding to the reports, a WhatsApp spokesperson said: “We are always working to stay ahead of those trying to abuse our service and ban accounts to help keep other users safe. Sometimes we get this wrong, and if we do, we try to fix it as quickly as possible to get people back to chatting.We’ve taken action to restore affected accounts."In this article, we explain possible reasons on why a WhatsApp account is banned temporarily, how to send a review request and other details.As explained on a WhatsApp FAQ page:“If you get a message in the app that your account has been “temporarily banned,” it could mean you're using an unofficial WhatsApp app or collecting information through a practice known as scraping”. It further states: “Download the official WhatsApp app or stop scraping after a temporary ban. Failure to do so could result in your WhatsApp account being permanently banned.”Follow the steps below to send a review request to WhatsApp:“We only review one phone number per appeal. If you don't see an option to request a review, this ban is permanent and cannot be appealed,” the FAQ page states.You can check the status of your request within WhatsApp. Keep in mind that contacting WhatsApp during the review process or through another user's account will not expedite the review process or affect the decision. Read this article to learn what to do after your account is unbanned.Readers must note that third-party services cannot ban or unban your WhatsApp account. Only WhatsApp can ban or unban a WhatsApp account.“We ban an account if we believe its activity violates our Terms of Service. For example, if an account is engaging in spam or scams, or if it compromises the security of WhatsApp users,” WhatsApp explained on its help page.You can't access your chat history or backups while your account is banned. You can only access your WhatsApp account backups if the phone number associated with the backup is unbanned.
Article Summary: Multiple WhatsApp accounts put under review for over 24 hours. Users reported seeing the following message on WhatsApp app screen: "Account in review. Date requested: 3 Aug 2026. Your account activity and device info is being checked to make sure it follows our terms of service. We will notify you of the result typically within 24 hours."

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: Chinese proverb of the day: "He who asks a question is a fool for five minutes; he who does not ask remains a fool forever"
Article Text:
What does the Chinese proverb mean?



Why asking questions matters

A lesson in humility





Relevance in today's world

A proverb with universal appeal

Timeless wisdom

Curiosity has long been regarded as one of humanity's greatest strengths, and few sayings capture that idea better than the Chinese proverb, "He who asks a question is a fool for five minutes; he who does not ask remains a fool forever. " At first glance, the proverb acknowledges the brief embarrassment that can come with admitting ignorance. Yet its deeper message is that refusing to ask questions carries a far greater cost because it prevents learning, growth and understanding. Whether in school, at work or in everyday life, the proverb encourages people to value knowledge over pride and to recognise that every sincere question opens the door to new ideas. Its wisdom remains just as relevant today as it was generations ago, reminding us that curiosity is often the first step towards personal and intellectual growth.The proverb teaches that there is no shame in asking questions. Most people have experienced moments when they hesitated to speak up because they feared appearing uninformed. The saying acknowledges that asking a question may briefly make someone feel self-conscious, but that discomfort lasts only a few minutes.Remaining silent, however, can leave a person without the knowledge they need for far longer.The proverb also highlights an important truth about learning: nobody is born knowing everything. Every skill, profession and area of expertise begins with a willingness to ask questions. Whether someone is learning a new language, mastering a musical instrument or understanding a scientific concept, curiosity is the foundation of progress. By encouraging people to seek answers rather than hide their uncertainty, the proverb promotes a lifelong love of learning.Questions are the foundation of education, innovation and personal growth. Every major scientific discovery, technological breakthrough and social advancement began with someone asking, "Why?" or "How?" Curiosity has driven explorers to discover new lands, scientists to develop life-saving medicines and inventors to create technologies that have transformed everyday life.In classrooms, students who ask questions often gain a deeper understanding of subjects than those who simply memorise information. A single thoughtful question can clarify an entire lesson and encourage discussion that benefits everyone. Teachers frequently view questions as signs of engagement rather than weakness because they demonstrate a genuine desire to understand.The same principle applies in the workplace. Employees who ask for clarification before beginning a task are more likely to avoid costly mistakes. Professionals who seek advice from experienced colleagues often develop their skills more quickly than those who pretend to know everything. In leadership, asking questions can foster collaboration, encourage fresh ideas and strengthen decision-making.Even in personal relationships, asking questions plays an essential role. Honest conversations build trust, reduce misunderstandings and help people better understand one another's experiences, perspectives and emotions.Another important message within the proverb is humility. Accepting that we do not have all the answers is a sign of confidence rather than weakness. In fact, recognising our own limitations is often the first step towards becoming wiser.People who are willing to admit they need help are usually more open to learning from others. They understand that knowledge can come from teachers, colleagues, friends or even strangers. By contrast, those who refuse to ask questions out of pride may limit their own growth because they avoid opportunities to gain new insights.Humility also encourages meaningful conversations. Instead of trying to appear knowledgeable at all times, people who ask questions create opportunities for discussion and shared learning. This approach strengthens teamwork, promotes mutual respect and allows everyone involved to benefit from different viewpoints.In an age where information is available at the touch of a button, asking the right questions has become more valuable than ever. Search engines, artificial intelligence tools and digital libraries provide access to vast amounts of information, but knowing what to ask remains the key to finding useful answers.The proverb is particularly relevant in a world where misinformation spreads rapidly through social media and online platforms. Rather than accepting every claim at face value, people should ask critical questions about the source, evidence and context of the information they encounter. Curiosity combined with critical thinking helps individuals separate facts from rumours and make informed decisions.The saying is equally important in professional settings shaped by rapid technological change. As industries evolve and new skills become essential, those who continue asking questions and embracing learning are often better prepared to adapt. Lifelong learning has become an important quality in almost every career, and curiosity remains at its heart.Although the exact origin of the saying is uncertain and it has often been attributed to Chinese wisdom rather than traced to a specific historical source, its message resonates across cultures. Similar ideas appear in many traditions around the world, reflecting a shared belief that the pursuit of knowledge is more valuable than protecting one's pride.The proverb's enduring popularity comes from its simplicity and practicality. It does not promise instant success or extraordinary achievements. Instead, it offers a realistic reminder that learning begins by admitting what we do not know. That lesson applies equally to children starting school, professionals building careers and older adults continuing to explore new interests.The enduring appeal of "He who asks a question is a fool for five minutes; he who does not ask remains a fool forever" lies in its timeless understanding of human nature. Fear of appearing uninformed is natural, but allowing that fear to silence curiosity can prevent personal growth and meaningful learning.Every expert was once a beginner who dared to ask simple questions. Every breakthrough started with someone seeking an answer that others had overlooked. By choosing curiosity over embarrassment and knowledge over pride, people give themselves the opportunity to grow throughout their lives. That is why this proverb continues to inspire students, professionals and lifelong learners around the world, reminding us that the shortest path to wisdom often begins with a single question.
Article Summary: The Chinese proverb, "He who asks a question is a fool for five minutes," is still relevant today. It encourages people to value knowledge over pride and to recognise that every sincere question opens the door to new ideas. The saying acknowledges that asking a question may briefly make someone feel self- conscious, but that discomfort lasts only a few minutes.

Article Title: How people in Chile's Atacama Desert evolved to survive drinking arsenic-poisoned water
Article Text:
Image: AI Generated

Why the Atacama Desert contains some of the world's highest natural arsenic levels

How scientists discovered protective genes that help Andean populations detoxify arsenic

Why the people of Quebrada Camarones carry more arsenic-protective gene variants

How 7,000 years of natural selection helped humans survive a toxic environment

Why the Atacama study changes scientists' understanding of human evolution

Why the people of the Atacama Desert remain one of humanity's most extraordinary evolutionary stories

For most of human history, a water source containing high concentrations of arsenic would have been considered deadly. Long-term exposure to the toxic metal is linked to cancers, cardiovascular disease, diabetes and neurological disorders. Yet for thousands of years, people living in Chile's Atacama Desert have relied on groundwater containing some of the highest naturally occurring arsenic levels ever recorded.The mystery has puzzled scientists for decades. How could entire communities survive for nearly 7,000 years without the public health crises normally associated with chronic arsenic poisoning? A study titled ‘ Human adaptation to arsenic in Andean populations of the Atacama Desert ’ by Mario Apata, Bernardo Arriaza, Elena Llop and Mauricio Moraga offers a compelling answer. Their research suggests that natural selection favoured genetic variants that help the body process and eliminate arsenic more efficiently, making the people of northern Chile one of the clearest known examples of humans adapting to an extremely toxic environment.The Atacama Desert in northern Chile is often described as the driest non-polar desert on Earth, but it is also one of the most geologically unusual.Volcanic activity over millions of years has released naturally occurring arsenic into groundwater, rivers and springs throughout the region. In Quebrada Camarones, where the study was conducted, arsenic concentrations exceed 1,000 micrograms per litre (µg/L), among the highest levels recorded anywhere in the Americas.For comparison, the World Health Organisation recommends a maximum arsenic concentration of 10 µg/L in drinking water. The water consumed by the Camarones population therefore contains arsenic levels more than 100 times higher than the modern guideline.Despite this extraordinary exposure, the region has not experienced the devastating epidemiological emergencies scientists would normally expect from such prolonged contact with arsenic.To solve this long-standing mystery, researchers compared the DNA of people from three regions of Chile with different histories of arsenic exposure.Mario Apata and his colleagues analysed genetic samples from 50 people in Quebrada Camarones, 47 from the Azapa Valley and 45 from San Juan de la Costa in southern Chile.The team focused on a gene called AS3MT, which helps the body break down and remove arsenic. They looked for four protective versions of this gene that are known to help people process the toxic metal more efficiently.By comparing how common these protective gene variants were in each population, the researchers hoped to find out whether thousands of years of living with arsenic-contaminated water had influenced human evolution.The results showed a clear pattern. People from Quebrada Camarones, who have lived with arsenic-rich drinking water for thousands of years, were much more likely to carry protective versions of the AS3MT gene than people from areas where arsenic levels are much lower.One protective combination of these gene variants, called the CTTA haplotype, was found in 68% of people from Camarones. In comparison, it appeared in 48% of people from the nearby Azapa Valley and just 8% of people from San Juan de la Costa, where drinking water has historically contained far less arsenic.The researchers also found that a gene variant linked to greater sensitivity to arsenic, known as the C variant of Met287Thr, was extremely rare in Camarones, appearing in only 1% of the population, but was more common in the other two groups.According to the researchers, these findings suggest that thousands of years of drinking naturally arsenic-contaminated water gradually favoured people with genes that could remove arsenic more efficiently, allowing those protective gene variants to become much more common over generations.The study provides one of the clearest examples of natural selection acting on modern human populations. Rather than developing immunity to arsenic itself, generations of people carrying gene variants that processed arsenic more efficiently were more likely to survive, remain healthy and pass those advantageous genes to their children.Over approximately 7,000 years, these beneficial variants became increasingly common within the population. As Apata, Arriaza, Llop and Moraga conclude, the high frequency of protective AS3MT variants in northern Chile indicates that efficient arsenic metabolism was likely selected as an adaptive mechanism, enabling communities to survive in an environment where safe drinking water was virtually unavailable.The findings demonstrate that human evolution is not confined to the distant past, it can continue wherever environmental pressures persist over many generations.The discovery extends far beyond arsenic alone. Scientists have long documented human adaptations to extreme conditions, including high-altitude living in the Andes and Himalayas, lactose tolerance in pastoral societies and resistance to certain infectious diseases.The Atacama research adds another remarkable example by showing that populations can also adapt genetically to long-term exposure to environmental toxins.Instead of relying solely on cultural solutions, such as changing water sources or treatment methods, which were unavailable thousands of years ago, these communities gradually evolved biological mechanisms that reduced arsenic's harmful effects.It is one of the strongest pieces of evidence that environmental pollution occurring naturally can shape the human genome over evolutionary timescales.For most of the world, water containing more than 1,000 µg/L of arsenic would represent a severe public health emergency.For the people of Quebrada Camarones, it became an evolutionary challenge spanning millennia.Their story illustrates the extraordinary ability of humans to adapt to some of Earth's harshest environments, not through sudden changes, but through countless generations of natural selection favouring traits that improved survival.The descendants of these ancient Andean communities still carry the genetic signatures of that long struggle today, offering scientists a rare glimpse into evolution in action and demonstrating that the human body can sometimes adapt to environments once thought impossible to survive.
Article Summary: People living in Chile's Atacama Desert have relied on groundwater containing some of the highest naturally occurring arsenic levels ever recorded. Long-term exposure to the toxic metal is linked to cancers, cardiovascular disease, diabetes and neurological disorders. People from Quebrada Camarones, who have lived with arsenic-rich drinking water for thousands of years, were more likely to carry protective versions of the AS3MT gene.

'Wildly insufficient'

Article Title: Quote of the day by JS Mill: 'I have learned to seek my happiness by limiting my desires, rather than...' and the 19th-century cure for modern burnout
Article Text:
John Stuart Mill was a 19th-century philosopher who argued that true happiness comes from developing the mind

I have learned to seek my happiness by limiting my desires, rather than in attempting to satisfy them.”

The breakdown of a calculating mind

The utilitarian paradox

Curbing the engine of infinite wants

A shopper standing in the middle of a brightly lit superstore, holding three slightly different versions of the same household item, often feels an odd sense of confusion rather than freedom. The endless scroll of online stores promises that the perfect product to complete life is just one click away. Yet, as packages keep arriving at the door, the promised happiness often disappears, replaced by a lingering desire for whatever comes next.This cycle of endless consumption is exactly what the Victorian philosopher John Stuart Mill described when he wrote: “Mill’s observation completely changes the usual idea of finding happiness. Instead of seeing human desire as an endless list of needs that must be fulfilled, he argued that desire itself is what needs to be controlled. Satisfaction, in his view, does not come from building a bigger net to catch every passing impulse, but from reducing what we expect and demand from the world.John Stuart Mill published this reflection in his Autobiography in 1873, a book describing one of the most intense intellectual upbringings in Western history.Born in London in 1806, Mill was raised under a strict educational experiment designed by his father, James Mill, and the founder of Utilitarianism, Jeremy Bentham. By the age of three, he was learning Ancient Greek; by eight, he was reading Herodotus and Plato in their original language; and by his early teens, he had mastered political economy and formal logic.The purpose of this education was to create a perfectly rational follower of Bentham—a person trained to judge every action by calculating how to produce the greatest pleasure and the least pain for the greatest number of people.The experiment seemed successful until 1826, when twenty-year-old Mill suffered a serious mental breakdown. In one of the most famous parts of his memoir, Mill recalled asking himself a simple question: if all his political and social goals were achieved tomorrow, would he truly feel happy? His honest answer was an immediate “no.” His highly rational way of thinking had left him emotionally empty.Mill’s recovery happened gradually, helped by the poetry of William Wordsworth and by a major reconsideration of Utilitarian philosophy. He realized that Bentham’s basic idea—treating happiness as simply the total of fulfilled desires—was deeply incomplete. To recover his peace of mind, Mill had to rethink what true well-being meant. The quotation from his Autobiography marks this important turning point, showing his realization that lasting happiness comes from controlling desire rather than satisfying every new craving.To understand Mill’s change in thinking, we must examine a tension within Utilitarian philosophy. Traditional Utilitarianism viewed happiness as the total amount of pleasure minus pain. If people could continue creating and satisfying new desires, happiness should, in theory, continue increasing.Mill recognized the major problem with this idea: human desires constantly grow. As soon as one desire is fulfilled, our expectations rise again, a pattern that modern psychologists call the “hedonic treadmill.” Trying to find lasting happiness by satisfying every new want is like trying to fill a bucket full of holes.By encouraging people to limit their desires, Mill was not promoting extreme self-denial or the lifestyle of monks. Instead, he brought his updated version of Utilitarianism closer to older philosophical traditions. Epicurus had argued centuries earlier that simple, easily achieved pleasures bring the greatest peace of mind, while Stoic thinkers such as Seneca believed that true wealth comes not from owning many things, but from wanting fewer things.Mill adapted this idea for the modern industrial world. He argued that higher intellectual and emotional pleasures—such as art, friendship, public service, and personal development—are naturally more valuable than endlessly collecting material possessions. Limiting material and superficial desires frees mental energy, allowing people to develop deeper, non-material sources of happiness that do not lose their value once they are achieved.In 2026, Mill’s insight speaks directly to one of the biggest challenges of modern life: the commercialization of human attention and desire. Today’s digital systems are carefully designed to constantly create new wants that can only be satisfied through more consumption. Targeted algorithms, personalized advertising, and micro-influencers work together to convince people that something important is always missing from their lives.The growing popularity of voluntary simplicity, digital minimalism, and anti-consumption movements reflects Mill’s principle in action. When technology workers switch to basic feature phones or consumers commit to “no-buy” years, they are putting his idea into practice. They are not doing so because they lack money, but because they want to break the endless cycle of constantly creating new desires.The same principle also applies to work and professional burnout. Modern workplaces often define success through constant growth: higher salaries, bigger teams, and continuous promotions. However, research in behavioral economics consistently shows that once people reach a comfortable middle-class standard of living, extra income brings smaller and smaller increases in everyday happiness. Executives who reject promotions to protect their personal lives or professionals who choose lower-paying jobs for better health are deciding to reduce their ambitions rather than spend their lives chasing ever-growing demands.By describing happiness as the relationship between what people have and what they want, Mill offered a lasting mathematical insight: the result can be improved either by increasing what you have or by reducing what you want.When Mill died in Avignon in 1873, he left behind writings that influenced modern liberal democracy, individual freedom, and economic thought. Yet perhaps his greatest personal achievement was overcoming the crisis of his youth. By understanding that peace of mind depends on controlling desire instead of constantly feeding it, he left a timeless guide for staying mentally balanced in a world designed to keep people forever wanting more.
Article Summary: John Stuart Mill was a 19th-century philosopher who argued that true happiness comes from developing the mind. He argued that desire itself is what needs to be controlled. Limiting material and superficial desires frees mental energy, allowing people to develop deeper, non-material sources of happiness.

Article Title: In 2018, a US engineer proposed spreading glass beads across Arctic ice to slow its melting; scientists later warned the plan could warm it
Article Text:
In 2018, a US engineer proposed spreading glass beads across Arctic ice to slow its melting. Scientists later warned the plan could warm it. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

The idea was to make the Arctic brighter

Scientists found a problem with the sunlight

Ice-albedo feedback. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

The debate over glass beads is still unresolved

The idea was deceptively simple: spread tiny glass beads across Arctic sea ice so their reflective surface could send more sunlight back into space. By making the ice brighter, proponents hoped to reduce the solar energy absorbed at the surface and slow the seasonal loss of sea ice.According to the study published in Earth's Future , in 2018, US electrical engineer Leslie Field and colleagues proposed just such an approach, known as surface albedo modification. Their idea involved spreading hollow glass microspheres, each only tens of micrometres across, over selected areas of young Arctic sea ice. The material was designed to float and reflect sunlight, much like a fresh layer of snow. However, the idea carried an important uncertainty. The effect of the beads would depend on how they interact with the changing Arctic surface and how much sunlight they absorb. Under some conditions, instead of increasing reflectivity, the material could absorb additional solar energy and contribute to warming.Arctic sea ice naturally acts as a giant reflector. Its bright surface sends a significant portion of incoming sunlight back towards space. When ice melts, the darker ocean underneath is exposed and absorbs much more solar energy.That additional heat can promote further melting, creating what scientists call the ice-albedo feedback.Field's proposal attempted to intervene in this process by keeping the surface reflective for longer. The proposed material was made of hollow glass microspheres, essentially tiny, lightweight silica spheres that can float on water. The 2018 study described experiments using commercially available glass microspheres on ice and snow, including tests in Minnesota and Alaska. The researchers argued that applying the material to young, relatively dark ice could increase its reflectivity and reduce the amount of solar energy absorbed by the surface.It was not about covering the entire Arctic with a literal layer of glass. The plan was to deploy the microspheres selectively in key regions such as the Fram Strait and Beaufort Gyre. The goal was to give young ice sufficient time to survive the summer period and turn into old ice, which would be highly reflective by nature.The study published in Earth's Future also states that climate modelling suggested that increasing sea-ice reflectivity could substantially increase ice thickness and concentration in some parts of the Arctic. The researchers presented the technique as a possible temporary climate intervention, rather than a replacement for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Yet the proposal depended on an important assumption: that the glass beads would make the surfaces they landed on brighter overall.According to research published in The Cryosphere , Arctic sea ice is not a uniform reflective surface. Its ability to reflect sunlight changes throughout the melt season as snow cover disappears and melt ponds develop on the ice. These ponds are darker than the surrounding snow and ice, reducing surface albedo and allowing more solar energy to be absorbed.The study also notes that the researchers used satellite observations from 2017 to 2023 to examine how melt ponds developed across the Arctic. They found substantial differences in pond coverage and development between regions and across the melt season. The study also shows that melt-pond formation is influenced by factors including air temperature and the physical characteristics of the sea-ice surface. The findings are important for understanding how sunlight interacts with Arctic sea ice. A surface that appears broadly white from above can contain a changing mixture of snow, bare ice and melt ponds, each with different reflective properties. As the melt season progresses, these changes can alter how much incoming solar energy is reflected and how much is absorbed by the ice and surrounding environment.The research does not examine glass microspheres or determine whether spreading them across Arctic sea ice would produce cooling or warming. Instead, it provides evidence for a broader point relevant to such proposals: the Arctic ice surface changes substantially during the melt season, so the effect of any attempt to alter its reflectivity would need to account for these changing surface conditions.The question of whether reflective glass microspheres could meaningfully slow Arctic sea-ice loss is more complicated than simply making the surface brighter. Research using satellite observations has shown that melt ponds can substantially alter the reflectivity of sea ice during summer. Their coverage also changes across regions and through the melt season, meaning that the amount of sunlight absorbed by the ice is constantly changing.According to Atmospheric Measurement Techniques, observations from airborne imaging have reached a similar conclusion. As snow begins to melt, its mixture of ice, water and air changes the way the surface reflects sunlight. This makes the performance of any reflective coating difficult to predict in the real Arctic. A material placed on bright, snow-covered ice would interact with sunlight differently from the same material on bare ice or a melt pond. Wind and melting could also change where particles remain on the surface. The result could therefore vary with the location, season and condition of the ice rather than producing a uniform cooling effect.It also raises a broader question: can an intervention that changes one part of a complex climate system produce predictable results as conditions change? And even if such a technique were eventually shown to preserve some sea ice, it would not remove the greenhouse-gas emissions driving the underlying warming. It would address one effect of warming, not the cause.
Article Summary: In 2018, a US engineer proposed spreading glass beads across Arctic ice to slow its melting. Scientists later warned the plan could warm it. The effect of the beads would depend on how they interact with the changing Arctic surface and how much sunlight they absorb.

Article Title: A 1990s Pizza Hut in Pennsylvania is still drawing crowds, and the real reason may be less about nostalgia than about the memories we attach to places
Article Text:
A branch of Pizza Hut in Blythe, California, with the distinctive red roof and corresponding logo | Wikimedia Commons

A branch of Pizza Hut in Blythe, California, with the distinctive red roof and corresponding logo | Wikimedia Commons

Why familiar places can feel surprisingly emotional

hiraeth

Pizza Hut Express location in San Marcos, Texas | Wikimedia Commons

Pizza Hut has discovered that memory can be good business

A red roof, stained-glass-style lamps, vinyl booths, and the familiar red plastic cups were all part of the vintage Pizza Hut experience back in the 90s. Surprisingly, a Pizza Hut in western Pennsylvania brings back a similar aesthetic, and the pizza alone doesn’t explain why some visitors are willing to drive for hours to eat there. The restaurant looks much the way thousands of Pizza Huts did during the 1980s and 1990s, before most of the chain shifted toward delivery and carryout. The location has turned into an unlikely attraction, and is a phenomenon psychologists have long recognized: places can become powerful triggers for autobiographical memories, reviving emotions and experiences that have little to do with the building itself. According to a report published by Phys.org , the Pennsylvania restaurant has become a gathering point for customers eager to revisit a setting that reminds them of childhood birthday parties, family dinners and the Book It! reading program that introduced millions of American children to Pizza Hut.Memory researchers have found that our brains don’t store experiences in isolation; instead, they become linked to sights, sounds, smells and locations that can later bring those moments rushing back with unexpected clarity. A restaurant or a neighborhood street often acts as a cue, which makes people feel as though they have briefly stepped into an earlier version of their lives.That helps explain why the Pennsylvania Pizza Hut resonates with visitors who remember more than just the food. They recall birthday celebrations under Tiffany-style lamps, the excitement of earning a free Personal Pan Pizza through Book It!, and evenings spent with family before smartphones became part of every meal. According to recent research published in the Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology , immersive experiences that recreate familiar environments can trigger vivid autobiographical memories and evoke, which refers to a longing for places and moments that can no longer be revisited exactly as they once were.Over the past several years, Pizza Hut and its franchisees have restored dozens of locations with signature features that had largely disappeared from the chain: the familiar red roofs, checkered tablecloths, salad bars, arcade games, and the oversized red cups that became an icon in the realm of family dining in the United States. The strategy has come at a time when the company is trying to reconnect with customers after restaurant closures and changing eating habits over the years. Industry reports show that some restored “Pizza Hut Classic” locations have become top-performing restaurants within their franchise groups, which attracts visitors who travel well beyond their local communities for the experience. The company has also revived its Book It! reading program and launched its “Hut Originals” campaign, both of which deliberately draw on memories shared by generations of customers.What draws visitors is rarely just architecture or décor; rather, it comes with a sense of nostalgia: a booth where someone celebrated a birthday, a salad bar they remember from childhood, or the glow of stained-glass lamps can reconnect them with people who are no longer around or moments that feel distant. Those emotional associations are difficult to replicate in newly built restaurants, which could explain why a surviving 1990s Pizza Hut continues to attract long lines decades after its design disappeared from most American towns. For many visitors, they’re not returning to eat the same pizza they remember; rather, they’re returning to a place that helps them remember a different version of themselves.
Article Summary: A Pizza Hut in western Pennsylvania has become a gathering point for customers eager to revisit a setting that reminds them of childhood birthday parties, family dinners and the Book It! reading program. The location has turned into an unlikely attraction, and is a phenomenon psychologists have long recognized.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:

Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.
